learning_architecture.rule: Build the knowledge layer like a good Psychology textbook: Unit as book, Topic as chapter, Micro-topic as a meaningful section/heading within that chapter. Each Micro-topic must be complete enough for its UGC NET/JRF requirement without being forced into a fixed checklist.

cross_references.purpose: Prevent micro-topics from becoming isolated silos and support mixed-concept NET questions.
rules: Cross-references are static content metadata stored with the canonical micro-topic record; never generate them in learner runtime.
Reference only canonical micro-topic IDs that exist in the syllabus.

Prefer high-value relationships such as prerequisite, contrasts with, often confused with, extension of, application of, same theorist/researcher, related construct, related method, historical progression, or theoretical alternative.
Do not create a link merely because two titles share a word.
A cross-reference should help the learner make or retrieve a meaningful conceptual connection.
Keep the learner-facing explanation itself coherent; cross-references are navigation/relationship metadata, not duplicate explanations.

levels.description: A UGC NET Psychology Unit is treated as a book-like knowledge domain containing related chapters/topics.
A Topic is a chapter within its Unit. It should form a coherent conceptual chapter rather than a loose container of unrelated micro-topics.
A Micro-topic is a meaningful heading/section within a Topic/Chapter. Its learner-facing content is a coherent article section that can stand on its own.

hierarchy.parts_note: Existing syllabus 'parts' may remain as navigation/grouping metadata where needed; they are not an additional learner knowledge level between chapter and section.

default_instruction:
CONTENT 2.0 — SOURCE-GROUNDED FULL REBUILD

Rebuild the complete canonical UGC NET Psychology learning library around the current learner architecture. The 549 canonical micro-topics in data/syllabus-index.json are the curriculum; do not create, delete, rename or renumber them.

SOURCE HIERARCHY
1. Authentic PYQs and official exam material establish exam intelligence: what NET actually asks.
2. Core Psychology textbooks establish conceptual accuracy, terminology, mechanisms, theories, evidence and depth.
3. Specialized Psychology sources add domain depth where relevant.
4. NET preparation books/notes may help exam framing but must not override stronger primary sources without evidence.

CONTENT PRINCIPLES
- Use the approved source library as the evidence base. Preserve source-supported terminology, distinctions, named researchers, theories, experiments, examples and organization where useful.
- The content may be extensive. Do not compress a concept merely to make it short. Where a source explanation is the clearest way to teach the concept, retain the necessary source-grounded detail.
- Do not silently fill source gaps with model knowledge.
- Do not invent PYQs, years, frequencies, trends, citations, researchers, experiments, statistics or claims.
- Synthesize sources when they genuinely complement one another and make disagreements explicit rather than manufacturing agreement.
- Remove generic AI filler, vague study advice and repetitive prose.
- PYQs are authentic exam evidence. Generated practice must remain clearly separate from genuine PYQs.

LEARNER ARCHITECTURE — NON-NEGOTIABLE
The learner-facing learning sequence is:
UNIT → TOPIC/CHAPTER → MICRO-TOPIC/SECTION → MICRO-TOPIC ARTICLE → OPTIONAL DEEP DIVE → CHECK ACTIVE RECALL → NEXT MICRO-TOPIC

On the micro-topic page:
- The Micro-topic itself is the canonical learner-facing article and must provide the complete NET/JRF-level understanding required for that section.
- The article is not a rigid checklist or a collection of mandatory fields.
- Do NOT force every article to contain the same headings, number of sections, examples, studies, comparisons or bullet lists.
- Use headings, paragraphs, bullets, tables, examples, comparisons, studies and other structures only when they improve understanding of that particular concept.
- Do NOT show Short Notes, an I Understand card, or a separate Detailed Explanation card as duplicate representations of the same knowledge.
- Do NOT restore the previous three-card bottom architecture.
- Deep Dive is optional enrichment beyond the NET requirement. It must add genuinely new, source-grounded depth rather than restating the Micro-topic article.
- The next learner decision after understanding is Active Recall, followed by the next micro-topic.
The backend may retain canonical micro-topic knowledge metadata and separate learning pools, but learner rendering must use prebuilt static content and preserve this textbook-like hierarchy.

CONNECTED LEARNING SYSTEM
UNDERSTAND = Deep Dive on the micro-topic page
RETRIEVE = Active Recall
APPLY = Practice
SPACE = Revision
MASTER = evidence-based mastery state
INTERLEAVE = meaningful static relationships between canonical micro-topics

DEEP DIVE
- This is the primary learner-facing explanation.
- Teach the concept properly, not as generic AI notes.
- Include definitions, mechanisms, theoretical background, researchers, experiments, distinctions, examples, applications, limitations, misconceptions and NET-relevant relationships whenever supported by the sources.
- Use clear hierarchy, paragraphs, bullets, tables or comparisons where they improve comprehension.
- Do not create a second summary that repeats the Deep Dive.

ACTIVE RECALL
- Test retrieval, discrimination, explanation and application of knowledge already taught.
- Never turn it into another notes page.
- Every answer must be recoverable from the taught content.

REVISION
- Reinforce the same knowledge through recall-before-review, weak-point identification and spaced scheduling.
- Do not introduce new facts.

PRACTICE
- Generate original learning questions that apply/discriminate the taught knowledge.
- Never label generated practice as PYQ.
- Use authentic PYQs only where they exist in the supplied question bank.

CROSS-REFERENCES
- Store meaningful static relationships between canonical micro-topics.
- Use only valid syllabus IDs.
- Prefer prerequisite, contrast, often-confused-with, extension, application, same researcher/theorist, related construct, related method or historical progression.
- Never duplicate the linked topic's explanation.

STATIC DELIVERY
All learner content must be prepared before learner rendering. The browser must only load and render prebuilt static content pools and indexes. Never call Gemini, generate explanations, infer source evidence, or assemble new learner knowledge at page-render time.

MICRO-TOPIC ARTICLE PHILOSOPHY
- Write each Micro-topic like a well-written Psychology textbook section or high-quality educational article, inspired by the clarity, conceptual progression and explanatory style of sources such as Ciccarelli/White and Simply Psychology, without copying their wording.
- The article must be self-contained and conceptually complete for the relevant UGC NET/JRF requirement.
- Completeness is judged by whether the learner can understand the concept accurately and answer relevant exam questions, not by the number of headings or points.
- Include only information that is necessary, useful or meaningfully clarifies the concept. Do not add a fact merely to satisfy a template.
- Let the topic determine the structure and length. A simple concept may need a short article; a complex theory, model, process or debate may require a substantially longer treatment.
- Build a logical teaching sequence: explain the idea, develop it, clarify important relationships/distinctions, and use evidence/examples only where they genuinely help.
- Where researchers, theories, mechanisms, experiments, applications, limitations, misconceptions, terminology or comparisons are necessary to understand or answer NET questions, include them naturally in the article.
- Do not treat these as mandatory sections for every Micro-topic.
- Avoid modular 'AI notes' language, repetitive labels, filler headings and fragmented fact lists.
- Do not turn the Micro-topic into an encyclopedia entry containing peripheral material merely because it exists in a source.
- Preserve important source-supported detail when it is needed for accurate understanding; do not oversimplify a concept merely to keep the article short.

DEEP DIVE PHILOSOPHY
- Deep Dive is not the longer version of the same Micro-topic article.
- Micro-topic = complete NET/JRF requirement; Deep Dive = optional understanding beyond NET.
- Deep Dive may add historical development, deeper theoretical reasoning, competing perspectives, broader research evidence, methodological nuance, debates, advanced applications or interdisciplinary connections when supported by the approved sources.
- Every Deep Dive addition must provide new learning value. If it only repeats the Micro-topic article, omit it.
- Do not force Deep Dive to exist for every concept if the approved sources do not provide meaningful beyond-NET enrichment.
user_instruction:
"user_instruction": "UNIT-WISE CONTENT 2.0 BUILD — UNIT 1

Rewrite the complete non-EXPERT-VERIFIED content library for Unit 1 only in this sequential build using the complete approved source library and authentic PYQ evidence.

CURRICULUM HIERARCHY
Treat the curriculum as:
Unit = book-like domain
Topic = chapter within the Unit
Micro-topic = meaningful section/heading within the Topic

The 549 canonical micro-topics in data/syllabus-index.json are the fixed curriculum. Do not create, delete, rename or renumber them. Preserve their Unit and Topic/Chapter relationships.

For each micro-topic produce one connected backend package:
- canonical micro-topic knowledge record
- learner-facing Micro-topic article that is complete for the relevant UGC NET/JRF requirement
- optional Deep Dive containing genuinely new beyond-NET enrichment when supported
- Active Recall
- Revision guidance
- original Practice MCQs
- meaningful cross-references

MICRO-TOPIC ARTICLE RULE
Write each Micro-topic as a coherent, readable Psychology textbook/article section. Do not use a rigid checklist. The article must contain all information necessary to understand the concept accurately and meet the relevant NET/JRF requirement, but must not contain unnecessary information merely to satisfy a template.

The structure and length must emerge from the concept. Use only the headings, paragraphs, examples, studies, researchers, theories, mechanisms, comparisons, applications, limitations, terminology and other elements that genuinely help explain that particular Micro-topic or answer relevant exam questions.

Do not produce fragmented 'notes' made of mandatory fields. Do not make every Micro-topic look structurally identical. Do not compress complex topics just to maintain uniform length.

DEEP DIVE RULE
Deep Dive is for learning beyond the NET requirement. It must add genuinely new, source-grounded understanding and must not merely paraphrase or repeat the Micro-topic article. It may cover deeper theory, historical development, broader evidence, debates, methodological nuance, advanced applications or wider conceptual connections when supported by the approved sources.

The learner must experience:
Micro-topic article → optional Deep Dive → Check Active Recall → Next Micro-topic

Never reintroduce Short Notes, I Understand, Detailed Explanation cards, or the previous micro-topic-page architecture.

This is a one-time full rebuild of the knowledge layer. Do not preserve shallow/generic existing AI wording merely for continuity. Keep accurate and useful material where it is source-grounded; substantially rewrite material that is generic, duplicated, unsupported, too shallow, or inconsistent with the new philosophy. Do not modify EXPERT VERIFIED components.

All generated content must be stored in the static content pools before it is exposed to learners.

CONTROLLED TEST TARGETS: 5-10-1 (Classical conditioning procedure), 5-18-3 (Working memory), 7-2-9 (Allport's trait approach).

SEQUENTIAL BUILD TARGET: Unit 1 — Emergence of Psychology. Process every canonical micro-topic in this Unit in syllabus order. Do not generate content for other Units in this run.",
